analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $4.55 over three years, with annual adjustments.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage increase passed both chambers — 248-171 in the House and 62-37 in the Senate — but President George H.W. Bush vetoed it, and the House override fell short, 247-178, when 290 votes were needed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps from $3.35 to $3.85, then $4.25, then $4.55 an hour, and created a review board to recommend annual adjustments after that. It also raised the sales threshold that exempts small businesses from minimum wage coverage, let employers count half of a tipped worker's tips toward the wage floor, and allowed a lower 'training wage' for brand-new workers for up to 60 days. A second title increased the amount Social Security beneficiaries aged 65-69 could earn before their benefits were reduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum, who would have seen their hourly pay rise by $1.20 over three years, plus beneficiaries aged 65-69 who could earn more without losing Social Security checks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid at or near minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.85 in 1990, $4.25 in 1991, and $4.55 in 1992 and after.
Sets up a Minimum Wage Review Board to review economic data annually and recommend adjustments, so the wage no longer erodes for years between congressional votes.
Increases the amount a Social Security beneficiary aged 65 to 69 can earn before benefits are reduced, and expresses the sense of Congress that the earnings limit be phased out by 2000.
Adds civil penalties for employers who repeatedly or willfully violate the wage and overtime rules.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers — restaurants, retail, and other service businesses — would bear the higher payroll, partially offset by a larger tip credit, a sub-minimum training wage, and a higher small-business exemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: The tip credit rises from 40% to 50%, meaning employers can count half of a tipped worker's tips toward the required wage, so part of the raise for tipped workers is paid by customers rather than the employer.

Employers may pay a brand-new worker a training wage below the new minimum — $3.35, or 85% of the minimum from 1991 — for up to 60 cumulative days, though it is capped at one-quarter of an establishment's hours and barred for farm workers.

The small business exemption threshold rises from $362,500 to $500,000 in annual sales, taking some small establishments out of minimum wage coverage entirely (those covered in 1988 must keep paying the old $3.35 floor and follow overtime and child labor rules).

The bill's own text orders studies of the increase's impact on rural and high-unemployment areas and directs committees to analyze employment effects of benefit mandates — an acknowledgment that supporters and opponents alike took the job-loss concern seriously.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a phased, moderate increase — about 35% over three years, when the wage had not moved since 1981 and prices had risen meanwhile. The offsets (a bigger tip credit, a temporary training wage, a higher exemption) trim the benefit for some workers, particularly tipped and first-time workers, but the core raise is real and the annual review board would have stopped the long erosion that usually happens between wage votes. The main honest objection is the standard one: opponents argued a higher wage floor costs some low-skill jobs, which is why the bill built in studies of exactly that question.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House and the Senate and survived a conference committee, but President Bush vetoed it in June 1989, and the House's attempt to pass it over his veto got 247 votes when 290 were needed.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 3, 1989 by Rep. Augustus Hawkins, the bill raised the minimum wage to $3.85, $4.25, and $4.55 in three annual steps and created a review board to recommend future adjustments.
The House passed it on March 23, 1989, 248-171, after the Education and Labor Committee reported it with amendments.
On April 12 the Senate struck the House language, substituted the text of S. 4, and passed it 62-37 — 52 of 55 Democrats for, 10 of 45 Republicans for.
A conference committee merged the versions; the House agreed to the report 247-172 on May 11 and the Senate agreed 63-37 on May 17.
The President vetoed the bill on June 13, 1989; the next day the House vote to override failed 247-178, well short of the two-thirds required.
Rather than a second attempt, the House referred the bill and veto message to the Education and Labor Committee, and no override followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The President and the opponents of the increase kept the federal minimum wage at $3.35 through the rest of 1989; low-wage workers got nothing from this bill, and employers of minimum-wage workers avoided the higher payroll.

for.name: 98 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, along with 2 of 175 House Republicans.

against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on June 13, 1989, after it passed both chambers.

against.name: 35 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on Senate passage and again on the conference report.

against.name: 178 House members
against.role: House members who voted against overriding the veto

sides.party_line_note: The Senate votes split sharply by party — 52 of 55 Democrats yes and 10 of 45 Republicans yes on passage, and 53-2 versus 10-35 on the conference report — while the House passed it 248-171 and the override failed 247-178, with Democrats providing most of the yes votes.

industries.industry: Restaurants and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: They would have had to lift the minimum hourly wage by $1.20 by 1992. The bill softened the blow for them: the tip credit rises to 50%, so employers count half of a tipped worker's tips toward the wage floor, and a sub-minimum training wage was allowed for new workers.

industries.industry: Small retail and service businesses under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: The exemption threshold rises from $362,500 to $500,000, freeing smaller establishments from minimum wage coverage; businesses already covered in 1988 are grandfathered at the old $3.35 rate with overtime and child labor rules kept.

The bill directs the Labor Department to treat hourly-paid computer systems analysts and software engineers earning at least 6.5 times the minimum wage as exempt professionals, so their employers would owe no overtime for them.
